title: Beauvoir's Second Sex
objective: After this level you can explain why Simone de Beauvoir wrote that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" and what she meant by woman as the Other.
summary: Beauvoir (1949) argued woman has been made man’s Other and shaped into a role of immanence; Spelman objected that she generalized from white, middle-class lives.

cards.headline: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.”
cards.body: Simone de Beauvoir wrote that line in The Second Sex in 1949. The book found eager readers and harsh critics; the Vatican put it on its list of prohibited books. What did the line mean?

cards.headline: Woman as the Other
cards.body: In The Second Sex (1949), Beauvoir argued that man casts himself as the Subject, the Absolute, the measure of what a human being is. Woman is defined against him as the Other: in her words, “the incidental, the inessential.” Measured by a male standard, women are then judged inferior.

cards.headline: Becoming a woman
cards.body: Her famous line targets the view that being a woman is simply a biological fact. For Beauvoir, women in her society were shaped into a role by social and historical conditions. Men got to express their freedom through projects, which she called transcendence, while women were pushed into repetitive, uncreative lives: immanence.

cards.headline: Accomplices, and critics
cards.body: Beauvoir didn’t paint women as mere victims. Many, she held, are partly complicit in being the Other, because the role brings benefits and spares them responsibility. Critics pushed from another side. Elizabeth Spelman (1988) argued that feminist philosophers, Beauvoir among them, treated white, middle-class women’s lives as all women’s, ignoring race, class and culture.

cards.headline: Beauvoir’s Second Sex: the big picture
learned: Man as Subject, woman as the Other
One becomes a woman through a social role
Spelman: she generalized from middle-class lives

questions.prompt: In The Second Sex, what role did Beauvoir say woman has been cast in?

options.label: The Subject, the measure of humanity
options.rationale: That is the role man gives himself.

options.label: The ruler of the household
options.rationale: Her claim is about being defined against men.

options.label: The Absolute
options.rationale: Man casts himself as the Absolute.

questions.explanation: Man casts himself as Subject and Absolute; woman is the Other, ‘the incidental, the inessential’.

questions.prompt: Why did Beauvoir say one “becomes” a woman rather than being born one?

options.label: Biology alone fixes a woman’s whole character at birth
options.rationale: That is the view her line attacks.

options.label: The law of each country defines who counts as a woman
options.rationale: Her claim is about social shaping, not legal definition.

options.label: Girls freely choose their role once they become adults
options.rationale: She describes a role imposed by society.

options.label: Social and historical conditions shape women into a role

questions.explanation: Her line targets the view that being a woman is a biological fact: women were shaped into a role by social and historical conditions.

questions.prompt: Beauvoir and Wollstonecraft (Level 55) both challenged a common view of women. Which one?

options.label: That women should be allowed to vote
options.rationale: Neither level’s argument is about the vote.

options.label: That women’s character is simply fixed by nature
That marriage should rest on friendship

questions.explanation: Wollstonecraft blamed false education and Beauvoir social conditions for what others called women’s nature.
